name: Stanford HAI AI Index page: annual AI data for policymakers
title: Stanford HAI AI Index page: annual AI data for policymakers
answer: This is Stanford HAI's landing page for the AI Index, an independent program that tracks, collates, distills and visualizes data on artificial intelligence for policymakers, researchers, journalists, executives and the public. Its most useful point for government readers is the claim that this year's Index shows a widening gap between AI capabilities and the frameworks needed to govern, evaluate and understand the technology. The page points to the 2026 report and related policy work, but it does not itself present government-specific metrics.

sections.body: Stanford HAI publishes this page as the landing page for the AI Index, an independent initiative at Stanford HAI. The page says the AI Index tracks, collates, distills and visualizes data relating to artificial intelligence, with a mission to provide unbiased, rigorously vetted and globally sourced data for policymakers, researchers, journalists, executives and the public. It describes a cross-sector lens covering research and development, technical performance, the economy, education, policy and more. The page was harvested on 2026-09-26 and refers to the 2026 AI Index Report, released this month, and to the 2026 AI Index. It also lists steering committee roles, related work, a collaboration and donation information.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The page states that this year's Index reveals a widening gap between what AI can do and how prepared we are to manage it. It says AI continues its rapid integration into the global economy, with technical capabilities improving, investment accelerating and adoption spreading, while the frameworks needed to govern, evaluate and understand the technology are falling behind. In a field where data transparency is declining, it argues independent, rigorous measurement has never been more critical. It calls the report the most comprehensive analysis of AI's trajectory available. The AI Index is described as a trusted resource for global media, governments and leading companies, equipping policymakers, business leaders and the public with insights into AI's technical progress, economic influence and societal impact. Previous editions, the page says, were cited in The New York Times, Bloomberg and The Guardian, have amassed hundreds of academic citations and were referenced by high-level policymakers in the United States, the United Kingdom and the European Union. The program is a collaborative effort led by an interdisciplinary AI Index Steering Committee from academia and industry. Related material includes a paper on measuring AI systems and their impact, based on a fall 2019 Stanford workshop, which identifies six summary challenges and summarizes over 40 presentations. The page also notes a collaboration with Dr. Elif Kiesow Cortez and the AI & LegTech Lab of The Hague University of Applied Sciences on regulatory frameworks and a judicial decision database.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The source states that previous editions were cited in The New York Times, Bloomberg and The Guardian, have amassed hundreds of academic citations and were referenced by high-level policymakers in the United States, the United Kingdom and the European Union. It says the related measurement paper identifies six summary challenges and summarizes over 40 presentations from a fall 2019 workshop at Stanford University. It refers to the 2026 AI Index Report, released this month, and to the 2026 AI Index. It names Dr. Elif Kiesow Cortez, the AI & LegTech Lab of The Hague University of Applied Sciences, Russell Wald and Sha Sajadieh. It gives no numerical counts for government policy measures.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: Readers following AI in government would use this page as an entry point to the AI Index program and its annual report, not as a direct source for government-specific metrics. The page says the AI Index is for policymakers and that previous editions were referenced by high-level policymakers in the United States, the United Kingdom and the European Union. It also describes policy as one cross-sector lens and notes a collaboration on regulatory frameworks and a judicial decision database. Those points make it relevant for understanding how an independent measurement program positions itself for policy audiences. However, the supplied text does not contain the government and policy track details cited on the industry page. A government reader should treat this as a signpost to the full report and related work, not as the evidence itself.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Government

sections.body: This is a landing page, not the full AI Index report. The supplied text is partial and truncated, and it does not include methodology, data tables, country-level government metrics or the government and policy track details. It is an institutional page from Stanford HAI, which says it relies on philanthropic support, and it includes a donation request. It refers to the 2026 AI Index Report as released this month and was harvested on 2026-09-26, but it does not give a separate publication date for the page. It is not a commercial product, but it is promotional in tone and points to other materials rather than presenting the underlying evidence.
